newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian vice president says Samper must go.
newsitem.headline: Colombian vice president says Samper must go.

text.p: Colombia's vice president on Thursday urged President Ernesto Samper to resign for the good of a country torn by growing economic problems and seemingly uncontrolled levels of violence.

"I believe that it is your inescapable duty as head of state to consider the certain and real possibility of resigning," Humberto de la Calle said in a open letter to Samper, read at a dramatic news conference on his return home from Spain where he recently stepped down as ambassador.
"This would allow for the formation of a government of national unity capable of leading the country on the crusade needed to salvage Colombia," the letter said.

In his letter, de la Calle said Colombia appeared to "falling to pieces" because of spiraling violence in the countryside, growing unemployment and a sharp economic slowdown that has led to "talk not just of a recession but of a collapse."

He added that the government had been severely weakened by charges that Samper used millions of dollars in drug money to finance his 1994 election campaign and was incapable of leading Colombia out of the ever-deepening crisis it is in.
"It is not viable to rule Colombia when you lack the capacity to call on most Colombians to defend what's left of the country," de la Calle said.

He added that a recent surge in leftist guerrilla activity added to the urgency of Samper's resignation since he had failed as the country's commander-in-chief to halt an unprecedented threat to "democratic stability."

"The security forces not only seem incapable of guaranteeing people's safety but must now watch as their own men are submitted to humiliating kidnappings," he added, referring to 60 soldiers who were seized as "prisoners of war" last Friday after rebels overran a military base in the country's southwest.
De la Calle, an ally of former President Cesar Gaviria, has never been close to Samper and has long been rumoured to despise him despite having served as his running mate in 1994.

He carries little political weight in Colombia, and his call for Samper's resignation is unlikely to represent anything more than an annoying thorn in the side of the thick-skinned Colombian leader, who has dismissed repeated calls that he step down in the past.
If de la Calle chooses to resign and lead the country's weak and divided opposition, political analysts say he could however become a major player in the country's 1998 presidential race.
And Samper's seemingly iron-clad control over Congress could be severely weakened by political infighting in the government, whether or not de la Calle remains in office.

In his open letter on Thursday, de la Calle urged all "democratic and renovating sectors" in Congress to block constitutional reforms that he said Samper was promoting with the support of "the most anachronistic and corrupt sectors of the old political class."
